idiom_name: constructor / dataclasses.replace copy published by rebinding one name or attribute
implementation_notes: Name binding (x = y) cannot be overloaded in Python; only attribute (__setattr__) and item (__setitem__) assignment can be intercepted, so the idiom becomes: build a complete new object -- dataclasses.replace, a new constructor call, or copy.deepcopy for a deep graph -- and publish it by rebinding the name, or by assigning the single attribute that holds the state. The new object exists in full before the old reference is dropped, so a failure while constructing or validating it leaves the current value untouched, and the collector releases the old object. Where an object really must change in place, define what state = value means in __setattr__ (or the store's own commit method) so that it is exactly one non-failing store; mutating a published mutable object in place is the form to avoid, because other holders see the change halfway through.
pitfalls: dataclasses.replace re-runs __init__ and __post_init__, and it does not carry over init=False fields (they are re-initialised, not copied), so a custom replace is needed when such fields must survive.

copy.deepcopy raises on members that cannot be copied (locks, sockets, open files, modules) and traverses the whole graph, which is expensive; the partially built graph is discarded, so the guarantee holds but the cost can be surprising.
frozen=True is shallow and escapable: tuple/dict fields are shared unless the update rebuilds them, and object.__setattr__ reaches around the guard entirely.

Rebinding inside a function only affects the local name, so a method that assigns self = new_value silently does nothing; the update must return the new object or store it on an owner (or mutate one attribute).
